extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory interested in causes that maintain democratic republics (e.g., historians, political scientists, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the principal factors Tocqueville identifies as supporting the maintenance and stability of democratic republics in the United States (institutional, social, economic, religious, and geographic causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of external threats / lack of military glory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have no neighbors, and consequently they have no great wars, or financial crises, or inroads, or conquest to dread; they require neither great taxes, nor great armies, nor great generals; and they have nothing to fear from a scourge which is more formidable to republics than all these evils combined, namely, military glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville explains the pernicious influence of military glory on republics by example (General Jackson: elevated chiefly by recollection of a victory). Where battles are rare, a single victory can have outsized political effects. Anti-pattern: populations prone to military glory become 'cold and calculating' yet dangerous to republican liberty. The absence of great external threats thus reduces the temptation toward militarization and charismatic military leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a great capital / no dominating metropolis
rubrics_metrics.description: America has no great capital a city, whose influence is directly or indirectly felt over the whole extent of the country, which I hold to be one of the first causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cities act as large assemblies whose populace can exert prodigious influence on magistrates and sometimes execute wishes without them. Tocqueville treats the lack of a single dominant metropolis as protective for a representative system; centralizing power in a metropolis risks placing the destiny of the state in the hands of a portion of the community acting on its own impulses. Example/contrast: European metropoles vs. U.S. distribution of cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and dangers of large urban lower orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower orders which inhabit these cities constitute a rabble even more formidable than the populace of European towns. They consist of freed blacks in the first place... They also contain a multitude of Europeans who have been driven to the shores of the New World by their misfortunes or their misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville warns that the nature of certain city populations (including freed blacks and impoverished immigrants) can threaten democratic republics via riots, corruption of local governments, and absence of effective control. He notes recent riots in Philadelphia and New York and predicts the peril unless the government creates an armed force under majority control but independent of town populations to repress excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal form of government (union of great power and small-state security)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal form of Government which the Americans have adopted, and which enables the Union to combine the power of a great empire with the security of a small State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed by Tocqueville as the first of three principal institutional causes maintaining the democratic republic. Implication: federal structure balances central strength with local autonomy, preserving republican principles while allowing collective action at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal institutions limiting majority despotism and teaching freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Those municipal institutions which limit the despotism of the majority, and at the same time impart a taste for freedom and a knowledge of the art of being free to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville names municipal (local) institutions as the second principal cause. They both restrain majority tyranny and train citizens in self-government. Guidance: strong local institutions are a check on centralized democratic excesses and an educational ground for civic habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution of the judicial power as a check on democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution of the judicial power. I have shown in what manner the courts of justice serve to repress the excesses of democracy, and how they check and direct the impulses of the majority without stopping its activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The independent judiciary is the third principal institutional cause. Tocqueville emphasizes courts' role in moderating democratic impulses—limiting excesses while allowing majority action—thus stabilizing republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the territory: abundant, open continent fosters equality and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief circumstance which has favored the establishment and the maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is the nature of the territory which the American inhabit... God himself gave them the means of remaining equal and free, by placing them upon a boundless continent, which is open to their exertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues physical geography (vast, fertile, underpeopled lands) provides opportunities that sustain equality and freedom: accessible land, natural resources, and space reduce pressures that produce social stratification. Example: North America offered an 'empty continent' rather than territories with dense settled populations to subjugate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous emigration / frontier movement preventing excessive parceling of property
rubrics_metrics.description: As a portion of the inhabitants annually leave the States in which they were born, the population of these States increases very slowly... The European emigrant always lands... in a country which is but half full, and where hands are in request... The law has abolished the rights of primogeniture, but circumstances have concurred to re-establish it under a form of which none can complain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes that regular westward emigration channels ambition and prevents estates from being divided to the point of insufficiency. This mobility produces social and economic opportunity (e.g., sons leaving to acquire land) and supplies capital and manpower for frontier development. Example: Connecticut furnishing many representatives to Congress born there but representing western states.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prosperity and favourable physical causes support democratic stability
rubrics_metrics.description: General prosperity is favorable to the stability of all governments, but more particularly of a democratic constitution... The physical causes, independent of the laws, which contribute to promote general prosperity, are more numerous in America than they have ever been in any other country in the world, at any other period of history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material well-being reduces incentives to overturn the state; abundance limits creation of new wants that could destabilize society. Tocqueville treats prosperity as an underlying stabilizer of democratic order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial passions and business habits shaping political life
rubrics_metrics.description: The passions which agitate the Americans most deeply are not their political but their commercial passions... they introduce the habits they contract in business into their political life. They love order... they set an especial value upon a regular conduct, which is the foundation of a solid business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that commercial spirit promotes prudence, order, practical calculation and respect for institutions; Americans favor practical, calculable policies over abstract theory. This temperament channels political activity toward stability and predictable governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a political institution that powerfully contributes to maintenance of democracy (including Catholicism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every religion is to be found in juxtaposition to a political opinion which is connected with it by affinity... The greatest part of British America was peopled by men who... acknowledged no other religious supremacy; they brought with them into the New World a form of Christianity which I cannot better describe than by styling it a democratic and republican religion... I think that the Catholic religion has erroneously been looked upon as the natural enemy of democracy... the Catholic citizens of the United States are at the same time the most faithful believers and the most zealous citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville presents religion (especially the Protestant-derived republican Christianity and, surprisingly, Catholicism under American conditions) as directly supportive of democratic equality: Catholic ecclesiastical structure levels laity under the priest; as a minority and often poor class, Catholics favor open political rights. He gives the priestly invocation at a public meeting as an example of religion mobilizing democratic sentiment. Guidance: religious institutions and beliefs can align moral duties with civic equality and support republican institutions when separated from governmental power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect influence of common Christian morality on manners and political utility of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian morality common to all sects—Influence of religion upon the manners of the Americans—Respect for the marriage tie—In what manner religion confines the imagination of the Americans within certain limits, and checks the passion of innovation—Opinion of the Americans on the political utility of religion—Their exertions to extend and secure its predominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that, beyond formal politics, the shared Christian moral framework across diverse sects shapes manners (e.g., respect for marriage, moral duties) and limits radical imagination, thereby checking revolutionary innovation. He notes that for society the precise theological tenets matter less than shared moral effects; this common morality is an indirect but powerful stabilizer of democratic life.
